source: Kim, He, Jain et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory
finding: A shared repository of agent trajectories (producers write, consumers retrieve) raised success and cut steps in ALFWorld and WebArena with no joint training. The authors call it transactive, but it is a shared retrieval store, not a who-knows-what directory.
numbers: ALFWorld success 47.1% no retrieval, 55.1% single-stage dense retrieval, 64.3% with SVMRank reranker (+17.2 points); steps 11.77 to 10.35. WebArena 18.2% to 20.5% (+2 to +2.3 points); steps 22.0 to 19.9-20.3. Index 86,833 chunks (ALFWorld), 20,102 (WebArena). Mean of 5 runs with randomized task-model allocation.
limits: WebArena gain is small, and one reranker (LambdaMART) fell back to baseline success. Two benchmarks, binary success. Only one retrieved trajectory chunk per call.
agent_relevance: Reusing other agents' experience helps even when the producer is not stronger. An experience store with similarity retrieval plus a learned reranker is worth building, but gains on hard web tasks are small.

source: Kim, He, Jain et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory - retrieval scope and ceiling
finding: Unrestricted retrieval beat same-task-type retrieval, which beat cross-task-type. Cross-task items still helped. Exact same-task trajectories give a big ceiling that the authors keep out of the main corpus to avoid leakage.
numbers: ALFWorld (274 tasks) success: full 64.6%, same task type 63.1%, cross type 59.9% (no retrieval 47.1%). WebArena (47 tasks): full 29.8%, same type 27.7%, cross type 19.1%. Oracle exact-task chunks (one consumer, GPT-OSS 20B, one seed): ALFWorld 20.1% to 38.7%; WebArena 16.6% to 40.4%.
limits: WebArena scope test has only 47 tasks. Oracle test is one seed and one consumer model.
agent_relevance: Much of the benefit of experience memory comes from near-duplicate tasks. Test any such memory with near-duplicates removed, or the gain is overstated.

source: Kim, He, Jain et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory - producer gap and scaling
finding: Consumers gained whether the producer was weaker, equal or stronger; the link between capability gap and gain was small and not significant. On ALFWorld gain grew with index size; on WebArena success dipped at a 50% index, then rose to 20.9% at full size.
numbers: 34 producers on ALFWorld. 3 producers made up 98.6% of the index, yet the other 31 supplied 31.8% of retrieved items; effective number of producers 2.2 in the index vs 10.5 in retrieval. Correlation of capability gap with gain about r=0.08-0.09, not significant.
limits: The WebArena non-monotonic curve is explained only by a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Producer metadata (a trust signal) carried some weight in the reranker, echoing the credibility part of human TMS. Do not assume the strongest source is the best source.

source: Wu, Luo, Liang, Shi, Ye, Payani, Shu (2026) Scaling Teams or Scaling Time? (LLMA-Mem)
finding: LLMA-Mem gives each LLM agent in a team three memories: episodic, procedural (consolidated) and transactive. The transactive memory stores agent profiles (specialization areas, task-type proficiency, collaboration history, success rate) and team patterns, and is consulted for task split, role assignment and team formation.
numbers: Tested on MultiAgentBench (coding, research, database) with Claude-Sonnet-4.5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-next-80B and Qwen3-32B. Token cost 9.4% to 71.7% lower than MARBLE and A-Mem baselines.
limits: No ablation removes the transactive module alone, so its separate effect is not measured.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM build of a who-knows-what directory, but its own contribution is untested. A directory of tool or sub-skill competence is cheap to keep, but needs its own ablation before we trust it.

source: Wu et al. (2026) LLMA-Mem - main results
finding: Gains in average score (AAS) were small and mixed. Coordination scores did not always rise when task scores rose.
numbers: AAS change vs no memory: +0.27 to +5.92 across model-environment cells (largest DeepSeek-v3.2 Research +5.92, Qwen3-32B Database +3.19, Qwen3-32B Coding +1.42). Qwen3-next-80B Research raised task score but lowered coordination, so AAS fell slightly.
limits: Single runs per cell, no confidence intervals in the text read. Many cells differ by about 1 point.
agent_relevance: Expect small gains from team memory; read 'consistent improvement' claims with care.

source: Wu et al. (2026) LLMA-Mem - topology and consolidation ablation
finding: Memory kept local to each role beat shared and hybrid memory. The authors say shared memory lets one role retrieve experience written under another role, causing incompatible reuse. This matches TMS: specialised stores plus a directory, not one flat pool.
numbers: Coding, Qwen3-32B-Instruct, consolidation interval 5: Local TS 49.68 / CS 46.69 / AAS 49.43; Shared 46.79 / 45.96 / 48.62; Hybrid 46.52 / 40.32 / 46.92. Interval: 2 gives TS 45.86, 5 gives 49.68, 10 gives 47.72, 20 gives 47.71.
limits: One model, one environment, differences of 1 to 3 points, no variance. MATM, by contrast, found a shared store helps.
agent_relevance: Keep separate stores per operator or state and route by a directory, rather than one flat memory.

source: Wu et al. (2026) LLMA-Mem - team size
finding: Bigger teams cost many more tokens and did not reliably do better; smaller teams with good memory sometimes beat larger ones.
limits: 16 research tasks only. Coordination score does not track task score.
agent_relevance: Splitting work over many copies of one model costs about 6 times the tokens for about 1 point on a strong model. Division of labour is not free for LLMs.

source: Shang, Liu, Liang, Zhang, Hu, Guo (2026) United Minds or Isolated Agents? (CoThinker)
finding: CoThinker uses a transactive memory module as a context-compression bottleneck: a manager distils consensus and each agent's expertise so agents do not re-read raw chat. Ablation: TMS helps one backbone and hurts two.
numbers: LiveBench Math subset. Qwen3-30B-A3B: TMS on + styles on 81.87; TMS on, styles off 69.79; TMS off, styles on 76.41. GPT5-Nano: 55.97 / 49.02 / 62.36. GPT-OSS-20B: 57.15 / 48.21 / 58.37. (The TMS-off, styles-off row is not in the table text.)
limits: TMS here is a summariser, not a who-knows-what map. Authors say newer GPT models refuse to give intermediate reasoning, which breaks the TMS prompt. Subset ablation, apparently single run.
agent_relevance: A compressed shared state helped one model (+5.5 points) and hurt two (-6.4, -1.2). Test per backbone.

source: Shang et al. (2026) CoThinker - perplexity proxy
finding: Perplexity of weaker models reading stronger models' answers fell sharply with the TMS summary.
numbers: Qwen3-8B perplexity: baseline 6.56, styles 3.58, TMS 1.69, 3 raw references 3.10. Mistral-7B: 6.63, 5.04, 1.58, 2.86.
limits: Perplexity measures ease of reading, not accuracy; a short generic summary also lowers it.
agent_relevance: A compressed summary is easier to absorb, but that does not prove it is more correct.

source: Shang et al. (2026) CoThinker - group size and similarity
finding: Agent count had a non-monotonic effect: more agents spread load but add coordination cost. Reading only similar peers risks echo chambers.
numbers: Agent counts M=6, 12, 18; reference-set size N in {0,2,3,4,5}; exploration rate in {0.1,0.3,0.6,1.0}.
limits: Figure-level results; exact values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Echoes G4: more copies of one model do not add independent knowledge.

source: Meta-analysis of collaborative inhibition: gender, membership, culture, memory monitoring (2024)
finding: Recalling together usually gives less than the pooled recall of the same people working alone (collaborative inhibition). This is the main challenge to a naive reading of transactive memory.
limits: Includes unpublished dissertations; high heterogeneity.
agent_relevance: Joint work can be worse than parallel solo work unless there is a directory and roles. Groups of identical agents are the stranger case.

source: Collaborative inhibition meta-analysis (2024) - relationship moderator
finding: Inhibition shrinks as partners know each other. The authors credit transactive memory (Wegner 1987).
numbers: Strangers k=46 d=0.75; acquaintances k=21 d=0.45; friends k=8 d=0.18 (ns); couples k=9 d=-0.19 (ns); QB=17.68, p<.001. Same-sex pairs d=0.64 (k=40), opposite-sex d=-0.11 (k=15, ns).
limits: Few couple and friend studies (9 and 8). Relationship is confounded with age and task.
agent_relevance: Closeness works through a shared directory. Agents from one model are like close partners without independent knowledge.

source: Collaborative inhibition meta-analysis (2024) - monitoring and culture
finding: When members could monitor recall, inhibition was not significant. The culture effect vanished in published-only data.
numbers: Without monitoring k=173 d=0.66; with monitoring k=12 d=0.14 (p=.20), mostly unpublished. Culture: Eastern d=0.47, Western d=0.76; published-only QB=2.31, p=.13.
limits: Only 12 monitoring studies.
agent_relevance: A checking step removes most group loss; fits G3 and G5.

source: Older long-married couples: collaborative facilitation and inhibition (2018)
finding: Couples recalled more together than the pooled solo recall for shared personal knowledge, but less for a word list on trial 1. Gain depends on task type.
numbers: 39 couples (78 people), age 68-90. Nominal vs collaborative: Word List T1 13.81 to 11.92 (inhibition, p<.001); T4 20.51 to 20.43 (ns); European Countries 26.56 to 29.79 (t(38)=4.94); Mutual Friends 30.85 to 47.64 (+16.79, t(38)=10.02). 2-year follow-up (32 couples): +2.91 and +12.84.
limits: Healthy, long-married Australian sample; nominal pools from a different session; no effect sizes reported.
agent_relevance: Memory sharing pays when partners hold distinct, relevant knowledge. For unshared lists, joint work hurts.

source: Older couples: strategy use and stability (2018)
finding: Benefit was a stable couple trait and related to strategy use and ability differences.
numbers: Benefit correlated across sessions r=.46 to .53. Strategy use vs benefit r=.37 (Mutual Friends), r=.35 (Word List T1), r=.15 (European Countries). Ability discrepancy vs strategy use r=.36.
limits: 32-39 couples; modest correlations.
agent_relevance: Explicit strategy, not mere co-presence, drives gain. The scaffold should set the strategy.

source: Ageing Together: memory compensation in long-married couples (2022)
finding: Real couples keep shared external memory and use each other as a resource. Division of labour is unequal.
numbers: 58 couples (116 people), age 68-90. 113 memory resources: shared ownership 52.1%, wife 27.4%, husband 20.4%; 38% (43/113) used indirectly through the spouse. External strategy mean 3.99 of 5; reliance 2.51; within-couple external score r=.71.
limits: Self-report and interview; older Australian sample.
agent_relevance: A TMS includes external stores plus pointers to who owns what; the directory holds pointers, not content.

source: Team curiosity, transactive memory systems, and team formalization (2026)
finding: Team curiosity predicted TMS and TMS predicted performance; the curiosity effect on TMS held only in teams with high formalization.
numbers: 87 teams, 406 members. Curiosity to TMS b=0.42 (p=.001); TMS to performance b=0.67 (p=.009); r(TMS, performance)=.29. Indirect effect 0.28, CI [0.05, 0.63]. Slope with high formalization 0.70, low 0.14 (ns).
limits: Cross-sectional survey; not checked whether all measures were from independent sources.
agent_relevance: A directory without a defined protocol did not help; fits our code-controlled transitions.

source: De Pasquale & Valcher (2022) Modeling the Cooperative Process of Learning a Task
finding: Control-theory model of TMS: each agent has an expertise level and an influence (appraisal) matrix that updates from perceived performance. With no stubborn agents, all converge to the highest expertise in the group; with stubborn agents, convergence depends on graph connectivity.
numbers: Expertise in (0,1]; row-stochastic influence matrix; expertise can only rise or stay; no agent exceeds the best initial expertise (stated in proofs). No empirical data.
limits: Pure math, not fit to data; assumes honest appraisals and free communication.
agent_relevance: Formal limit: a team learns up to its best member and no further. A team of copies of one model cannot exceed that model.

source: Meske, Hermanns, Brachten (2026) The GenAI Who Knew Too Little
finding: Interviews: TMS between people and GenAI differs from human TMS. Humans learn the AI's skills, the AI keeps only temporary track of human expertise, trust is ambivalent, and coordination runs one way.
numbers: 14 knowledge workers, qualitative thematic analysis. Three dimensions (specialization, credibility, coordination) per Lewis & Herndon 2011.
limits: Small interview sample; self-report; no performance measure.
agent_relevance: The AI side of the directory is missing: models lack metamemory of the user. A scaffold must supply it as an explicit state.

source: Akgun & Toker (2026) When Does GenAI Use Support Critical Thinking?
finding: In a structural model, GenAI experience raised critical thinking only through dividing and coordinating labour with the tool and through reworking its output. Direct effects were not significant.
numbers: N=891 students (US and Turkey). Fit chi2(8)=24.258, CFI=.974, RMSEA=.048. Familiarity to Specialization&Coordination b=.636; to Reflective Transformation b=.367; Spec&Coord to CT .230 (p=.002); Reflective to CT .175 (p=.007); direct paths ns. Total indirect .211.
limits: Cross-sectional self-report; students; critical thinking self-rated.
agent_relevance: Dividing work with a tool helps only when paired with reworking its output; matches G2.

source: Wikipedia: Transactive memory (secondary summary)
finding: Secondary summary of human findings: groups trained together outperformed groups trained apart; teammate-skill feedback alone raised TMS and performance; familiarity or liking did not explain the gap; coordination, specialization and credibility are the Lewis 2003 scale parts.
numbers: No numbers on the page. Cites Liang, Moreland & Argote 1995; Moreland et al. 1996; Moreland & Myaskovsky 2000; Hollingshead 1998, 2001; Lewis 2003, 2004; Ren & Argote 2011.
limits: Encyclopedia page; primary papers paywalled here.
agent_relevance: Knowing who is good at what helps even without interaction. Directory content matters, not only talk.

source: Wikipedia: Google effect (secondary) - Sparrow, Liu & Wegner 2011 and replications
finding: The 'internet as transactive memory' result was listed as not replicated in the Camerer 2018 project; later work found it only when people had prior experience that saved items stay accessible; a 35-study meta-analysis (Gong & Yang 2024) supports a version of it.
numbers: Camerer et al. 2018 (21 Nature/Science experiments): not replicated. Gong & Yang 2024: 35 studies. No effect sizes on the page.
limits: Secondary source with no numbers.
agent_relevance: Use 'remember where, not what' as a design hint only.

source: Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory
finding: Four experiments: people who expect to look information up later remember it less but remember where it is stored better. Only the abstract line was seen (Crossref).
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
quote: Owing to Internet search, we are more likely to encode 'where' aspects of memory rather than 'what.'
limits: Not opened (paywall). Replication failure per Camerer 2018.
agent_relevance: Pointers beat content when external access is reliable.

source: Wegner (1987) Transactive memory: a contemporary analysis of the group mind
finding: Founding chapter. Transactive memory is personal memories plus transactive processes (encoding, storage, retrieval across people), built on a directory of who knows what (labels and locations) and differentiated responsibility. Description taken from secondary text (Meske 2026), not from the chapter.
numbers: No numbers; theory chapter.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Three-step directory design: update the directory, hold pointers, route a question to the right holder.

source: Wegner, Erber & Raymond (1991) Transactive memory in close relationships
finding: Couples vs stranger pairs under free vs imposed memory structure. From memory, not read: natural couples did better when free to divide as they wished and worse when an imposed structure clashed with their own division.
numbers: Numbers not verified.
limits: Not opened; recollection only.
agent_relevance: Imposed structure can break a division of labour that already works.

source: Lewis (2003) Measuring transactive memory systems in the field
finding: Scale with three parts: specialization, credibility, coordination; widely used since. Page not read; parts confirmed by Meske 2026 and Wikipedia.
numbers: Numbers not verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Three directory-quality checks for an agent: knows who is expert, trusts them, coordinates.

source: Liang, Moreland & Argote (1995) Group versus individual training and group performance
finding: Teams trained together developed stronger TMS, recalled more and made fewer errors than teams trained apart (per the Wikipedia summary; the original was not read).
numbers: Numbers not verified.
limits: Not opened; URL points to the secondary page.
agent_relevance: Shared practice builds the directory.
